lines.say: A population is one species, in one area, at one time.
Size changes by births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
The per capita rate of increase, r, is births minus deaths per individual.
Spacing can be clumped, uniform or random. Territories often make it uniform.
With unlimited resources, growth is proportional to N. A J curve.
To predict a size, use N t equals N nought e to the r t.
50 wallabies, r is 0.4, for 5 years. That's 50 times e squared.
About 369 wallabies. But it can't go on forever.
Doubling time is about 0.693 divided by r.
Carrying capacity, K, is the most the environment can support long term.
The logistic model slows growth by the fraction of K still unused.
At N equals 200, with K 1000: 0.4 times 200 times 0.8. That's 64 per year.
Growth peaks at half full, like a car park. At 500, the rate is 100.

draw.alt: S-curve levelling off at K, steepest at K/2

lines.say: At K, growth stops. Real populations often overshoot and oscillate.
Density dependent factors hit harder when crowded: competition, disease, predation.
Density independent factors hit the same share regardless: floods, frost, fire.
Only density dependent factors can regulate a population near K.
r selected: early, many small offspring, little care. K selected: the opposite.

draw.alt: Many small offspring versus few large offspring

lines.say: Richness is how many species. Evenness is how equally they're spread.
Only about 10 percent of energy passes to each next trophic level.
A keystone species has a huge effect for its numbers. Remove the sea star, and mussels take over.
Primary succession starts on bare rock. Lichens and mosses build soil.
Secondary succession starts where soil remains, like after fire. It's faster.
Intermediate disturbance often gives the highest richness.
Simpson's D is a two pick test: the chance two are different species.
Site 1 has 10 of each of 4 beetles. D is 0.769.

draw.alt: Even site with four equal bars

lines.say: Site 2 has 37 of one species and 1 of each other. D drops to 0.146.

draw.alt: Even site beside site dominated by one species

lines.say: Same richness, very different diversity. Evenness matters.
The Shannon index also rises with richness and evenness.
r is per individual. d N d t is the whole population's growth rate.
Growth isn't fastest at K. It stops there. It's fastest at half K.
K isn't fixed for a species. It changes with the environment.
